title: THE BIBLE’S MOST UNCOMFORTABLE SEXUAL LAWS REQUIRE CONTEXT—NOT EMBARRASSMENT, NOT EXCUSES.
paragraphs: THE BIBLE’S MOST UNCOMFORTABLE SEXUAL LAWS REQUIRE CONTEXT—NOT EMBARRASSMENT, NOT EXCUSES.

Some passages sound so disturbing that Christians avoid reading them aloud. Critics use them to accuse God. Believers sometimes rush to defend what they have never studied. But what happens when we stop hiding from the difficult verses, open the ancient Hebrew Scriptures, and discover that understanding the Bible honestly may lead us straight to the heart of Jesus Christ?
There is a moment that can shake a Christian's faith without warning.
Someone opens the Bible, reads a verse about sexual violence, marriage, virginity, or a woman's place in ancient Israel, and asks a question that suddenly makes the entire room uncomfortable.
“Wait. Did God really command that?”
The confident believer goes quiet.
The skeptic leans forward.
The person who has survived sexual abuse feels something tighten inside their chest.
And somewhere in the conversation, somebody says the words Christians should never be afraid to hear:
“Can you explain this without making excuses?”
That question deserves more than a rehearsed answer.
Because if the Bible really is God's Word, we should not have to protect it by pretending its hardest passages are easy.
And if Jesus Christ really is the truth, then honest examination is not His enemy.
But before we go any further, understand something.

This article will not pretend that ancient Israel operated under modern laws. It will not claim every Old Testament regulation represents God's ideal for human relationships. It will not excuse sexual violence, erase women's suffering, or turn difficult Hebrew words into convenient translations.
We are going to open the passages people often avoid.
And we are going to ask what they actually say.
Not what a viral screenshot claims.
Not what an embarrassed Christian wishes they said.
Not what an angry critic assumes they must mean.
What the text says. What the language means. What the historical setting reveals. And how Christians should understand these passages in the light of Jesus Christ.
Because sometimes the most dangerous thing you can do with Scripture is not question it.
It is quote it without understanding it.
Consider Deuteronomy 22.

Within a relatively short section, we encounter laws about accusations of premarital sexual activity, adultery, sexual assault, betrothal, and a man who has sexual relations with an unbetrothed virgin.
These are not comfortable verses.
They were never intended to become inspirational wall decorations.
They belong to an ancient legal collection addressing real disputes in a society radically different from ours.
And the first mistake readers make is treating every law in that collection as though it were a direct instruction to every Christian living today.
That is not how biblical interpretation works.
The Hebrew word תּוֹרָה (torah) can mean instruction, teaching, or law, depending on context. The Torah contains commands, narratives, covenant obligations, and legal provisions given to Israel.
Those laws operated within Israel's particular covenant and social world.
They must be read according to their literary context, their historical setting, and their place in the unfolding biblical story.
This matters because a law regulating a damaged human situation does not automatically mean God delights in the situation being regulated.
Jesus Himself established this distinction.
When religious leaders questioned Him about divorce, He answered:
“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.” — Matthew 19:8, KJV
Read that again.
“From the beginning it was not so.”
Jesus distinguished between a legal concession made in response to human hardness and God's original intention for marriage.
That does not mean every difficult Old Testament law can simply be dismissed as a concession. Each passage still requires careful interpretation.
But it establishes something enormously important.
A biblical law may address human brokenness without presenting that brokenness as God's perfect design.
And suddenly, we have a better question to ask.
Not merely, “Why does this law exist?”
But, “What problem was this law addressing, what did it require in its original setting, and how does it relate to God's larger purposes?”
Now consider one of the most disturbing accusations made against the Bible.
“Doesn't the Bible command a rape victim to marry her rapist?”
The passage usually cited is Deuteronomy 22:28–29.

In the King James Version, it describes a man who finds an unbetrothed virgin, lays hold of her, and has sexual relations with her. The man must pay fifty shekels of silver to her father, and the text says she becomes his wife and that he may not divorce her.
That is what the passage says.
And we must not pretend it says something softer.
The Hebrew wording deserves close attention.
In Deuteronomy 22:25, describing a man who sexually assaults a betrothed woman in the countryside, the verb is וְהֶחֱזִיק (vehecheziq), from a root associated with taking hold of or overpowering.
But in Deuteronomy 22:28, the expression is וּתְפָשָׂהּ (utefasah), from תָּפַשׂ (taphas), meaning to seize, grasp, or take hold of.
These are different Hebrew verbs.
That difference matters.
But here is where honesty becomes essential.
The difference alone does not prove that the second encounter was consensual.

The verb taphas can describe forceful taking, and interpreters disagree about whether Deuteronomy 22:28–29 addresses rape, another form of coercive sexual misconduct, or illicit intercourse in a setting where the woman's consent is not specified.
We should not claim that Hebrew grammar settles a question it does not settle.
And we should not erase the troubling fact that the law is framed within a patriarchal social and legal system.
Exodus 22:16–17 provides a related law involving a man who seduces an unbetrothed virgin. There, the woman's father can refuse to give her in marriage.
That related passage is important context.
But it does not explicitly resolve every question about Deuteronomy 22:28–29, and we should not automatically import every provision from Exodus into Deuteronomy as though the texts were identical.

Some Christian interpreters understand the Deuteronomy law as imposing lifelong financial and marital responsibility on a man who has seriously wronged a woman in a society where marriage strongly affected her economic security.
Others argue that the passage reflects an ancient legal framework that does not adequately address the woman's consent or autonomy by modern standards.
Those concerns cannot be brushed aside.
The text imposes a penalty and an obligation on the man. It does not explicitly say the woman is free to refuse the marriage.
We cannot honestly claim that it does.
But neither should we confuse an ancient legal provision with a universal Christian command that victims of sexual assault must marry their attackers.
No Christian pastor, parent, or church should use this passage to pressure a sexual assault survivor into marrying or remaining with an abuser.
That would be a grievous misuse of Scripture.
And if you have ever heard this passage used to silence your pain, please hear this clearly.
Your suffering is not an inconvenience to biblical interpretation.
You are a human being made in the image of God.
What happened to you matters.
And the Gospel never requires you to call evil good.
Now look at the immediately preceding law.
Deuteronomy 22:25–27 addresses a betrothed woman assaulted in the countryside.
The law holds the attacker responsible and explicitly says that the woman has committed no offense deserving death.
The passage compares the assault to a man rising against his neighbor and killing him.
That comparison is astonishingly serious.
The Hebrew text in verse 26 says:
וְלַנַּעֲרָ לֹא־תַעֲשֶׂה דָבָר
Vela-na'arah lo-ta'aseh davar.
“Do nothing to the young woman.”
The passage continues by stating that she has no sin deserving death.
In its ancient legal context, the law recognizes her innocence and treats the assault as a grave act of violence.
Notice what the text does not say.
It does not blame her for being attacked.
It does not declare her morally contaminated by another person's violence.
It does not say that the crime becomes less serious because the attacker desired her.
It places guilt upon the offender.
That is a vital distinction.

Yet we should also recognize that Deuteronomy 22:23–24, dealing with an assault or sexual encounter involving a betrothed woman in a city, raises serious questions about assumptions concerning whether she could have cried out or obtained help.
We must not turn those ancient assumptions into modern tests of whether someone has been assaulted.
Survivors may freeze, become unable to speak, comply out of fear, or be physically prevented from resisting.
The absence of a scream does not establish consent.
A faithful Christian reading must never weaponize an ancient evidentiary assumption against a person seeking protection today.
And perhaps this is where some of us need to repent.
Not because we asked difficult questions about the Bible.
But because we sometimes answered them without compassion.
We were so desperate to win an argument that we forgot there might be a wounded person listening.
Someone who has spent years wondering whether God cared about what happened behind a locked door.
Someone whose attacker used religious language.
Someone who was told to remain silent to protect a family's reputation.
Someone who heard more concern for a ministry's image than for their own safety.
If that is you, I want you to know that defending the Bible does not require defending the person who harmed you.
And protecting the reputation of a religious institution is not the same thing as honoring Jesus Christ.
There is another passage that demands this same honesty.
Numbers 5:11–31 describes the ordeal of a woman whose husband suspects her of adultery but lacks evidence.
The passage involves a priest, an oath, and a ritual using water mixed with dust from the tabernacle floor.
Some modern readers describe this as a biblical abortion ritual.
Others insist it has nothing whatsoever to do with reproductive consequences.
Both claims can oversimplify a difficult text.
The Hebrew passage includes the expression וְנָפְלָה יְרֵכָהּ (venafelah yerekhah), literally involving her thigh falling or wasting, alongside language concerning her abdomen swelling.
The word יָרֵךְ (yarekh) ordinarily means thigh, but can function euphemistically in contexts involving reproduction or descendants.
Scholars debate the precise physical consequence envisioned.
Some understand the language as referring to reproductive injury, infertility, or miscarriage. Others interpret it differently.
The text does not describe a physician performing a modern medical abortion procedure. Nor does it provide a straightforward basis for claiming that the passage settles contemporary abortion ethics.
Its ancient setting is a ritual ordeal addressing suspected infidelity where ordinary evidence was absent.
The ritual places the outcome under divine judgment rather than authorizing the husband to impose punishment on his own suspicion.
That distinction matters.
So does the fact that the passage centers on a husband's suspicion and does not provide an equivalent ritual for a wife suspecting her husband.
We do not need to conceal that asymmetry.
Context should make our reading more truthful, not more convenient.
And then there is Leviticus 18.
A chapter filled with prohibitions involving incestuous relationships, adultery, same-sex intercourse between males, and sexual relations with animals.
Some readers treat it as though every command can be applied directly without examining the covenantal setting.
Others dismiss the entire chapter as irrelevant ancient material.
Neither approach adequately accounts for the Bible's complexity.
Leviticus 18 belongs to Israel's holiness legislation.
Its concern is not merely individual desire but the identity and conduct of a people called to live differently from the surrounding nations.
Leviticus 18:6 begins with a prohibition against approaching close relatives to uncover their nakedness.
The Hebrew expression לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה (legalot ervah) means “to uncover nakedness,” a legal idiom frequently referring to prohibited sexual relations.
Understanding that expression helps us recognize that the passage is not simply about accidental exposure or ordinary nudity.
It is addressing sexual boundaries.
Leviticus 18:22, meanwhile, prohibits a male lying with another male in the manner described as lying with a woman.
The Hebrew reads:
וְאֶת־זָכָר לֹא תִשְׁכַּב מִשְׁכְּבֵי אִשָּׁה
Ve'et-zakhar lo tishkav mishkevei ishah.
A close rendering is:
“You shall not lie with a male as with the lyings of a woman.”
Christians disagree about how this prohibition should be related to modern understandings of sexual orientation, committed same-sex relationships, and New Testament teaching.
Traditional Christian interpreters generally understand the prohibition as part of a continuing biblical sexual ethic reserving sexual intercourse for marriage between a man and a woman.
Other interpreters argue that the ancient social setting, the nature of the acts envisioned, and the relationship between Israel's holiness laws and Christian ethics require a different conclusion.
We should state those disagreements accurately rather than pretending they do not exist.
And whatever conclusions Christians reach, no one is given permission to humiliate, assault, threaten, or dehumanize another person.
Every person bears the image of God.
Biblical conviction does not cancel the command to love one's neighbor.
And love does not require dishonesty about what we believe Scripture teaches.
The challenge is to hold truth and compassion together without turning either into a weapon.
Now consider another passage that can make modern readers recoil.
Deuteronomy 21:10–14 describes an Israelite man who desires to marry a woman taken captive during war.
The woman is permitted a period of mourning. The man is instructed to follow a prescribed process before marriage, and if he later rejects her, he must let her go freely rather than sell her.
Some defend this passage by pointing out that it places restrictions upon the treatment of a captive woman.
And it does.
But the woman is still a captive.
The circumstances are shaped by war, defeat, and an enormous imbalance of power.
The passage does not explicitly describe her free consent to the marriage.
That is morally troubling.
Acknowledging it is not rebellion against God.
It is taking the words seriously enough to refuse to invent protections the passage never explicitly states.
We can recognize that the law restrains certain abuses within its ancient context without presenting the whole arrangement as the ideal of Christian marriage.
The biblical story does not end with ancient warfare or the legal structures of Israel.
It moves toward Jesus Christ.
And that changes how Christians must approach the whole conversation.
Because when Jesus speaks about marriage in Matthew 19, He reaches behind the Mosaic divorce regulation to Genesis.
To creation.
To the beginning.
Before conquest.
Before monarchy.
Before the accumulated damage of generations of human sin.
Genesis 1:27 declares that God created humanity in His image, male and female.
Genesis 2:24 describes the man and woman becoming one flesh.
Jesus cites this creation account in Matthew 19:4–6.
And in doing so, He points to a vision of marriage grounded in God's creative intention rather than merely the management of human brokenness.
But even here, we must be careful.
Jesus does not invite us to romanticize marriage while ignoring violence inside it.
A marriage certificate does not make cruelty holy.
A wedding vow does not transform sexual coercion into love.
And the command to forgive does not require a victim to abandon safety, refuse justice, or immediately restore trust.
Forgiveness, repentance, reconciliation, and accountability are related concepts, but they are not interchangeable.
The New Testament commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her (Ephesians 5:25).
That is sacrificial love.
Not domination disguised as leadership.
Not entitlement disguised as covenant.
Not control disguised as spiritual authority.
A man who quotes Scripture to justify harming his wife is not demonstrating Christlike headship.
He is contradicting the self-giving pattern that passage commands.
And if someone needs immediate protection from abuse, seeking safety and appropriate professional or legal help is not a failure of faith.
Now watch Jesus in John 8.
Religious leaders bring before Him a woman accused of adultery.
They invoke the Law of Moses.
They want a judgment.
But the scene is more complicated than the familiar retelling often admits.
The passage known as John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel and appears in different locations in portions of the manuscript tradition.
Many Christian Bibles include it with a textual note.
That manuscript issue matters, and responsible interpretation should acknowledge it.
The story itself, as preserved in the Christian tradition, portrays Jesus confronting accusers who seek to trap Him while showing mercy toward the accused woman.
He says:
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.” — John 8:7, KJV
One by one, the accusers leave.
Then Jesus says:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Mercy.
And a call to changed living.
Not permission to continue in sin.
Not delight in public humiliation.
And certainly not indifference toward the truth.
But we should not build the entire biblical doctrine of sexual ethics upon a passage with a disputed textual history.
The broader, securely attested New Testament already shows Jesus extending mercy to sinners, confronting hypocrisy, calling people to repentance, and refusing to treat the vulnerable as disposable.
Look at Luke 7:36–50.
A woman known in the city as sinful approaches Jesus while He is dining in a Pharisee's home.
She weeps at His feet.
The religious host silently questions whether Jesus understands what kind of woman is touching Him.
Jesus does understand.
And He sees what the Pharisee does not.
A repentant heart.
Love.
Faith.
The terrible weight of a life that needs forgiveness.
Jesus tells her:
“Thy sins are forgiven.” — Luke 7:48, KJV
And later:
“Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.” — Luke 7:50, KJV
Can you imagine hearing those words after years of shame?
Not from someone trying to use you.
Not from someone collecting your mistakes as ammunition.
Not from someone who wants to make your past your permanent identity.
But from Jesus.
“Go in peace.”
Perhaps you have never been publicly accused of sexual sin.
But you know what it means to carry a secret.
The relationship you knew was wrong.
The pornography you keep returning to.
The betrayal you have hidden.
The intimacy you offered because you were afraid someone would leave.
The manipulation you endured because you thought you had no other choice.
The guilt you feel about something you willingly did.
Or the shame you have been carrying for something that was done to you.
Those last two experiences are not the same.
Sin requires repentance.
Abuse requires protection, truth, and justice.
A person assaulted against their will does not need to repent for being assaulted.
And no one should confuse the shame imposed by a perpetrator with the conviction of the Holy Spirit.
Yet both the guilty and the wounded need to know that Jesus is not indifferent to their lives.
The guilty need forgiveness and transformation.
The wounded need compassion, safety, and healing.
And some people carry both kinds of pain from different experiences.
That is why simplistic answers fail.
Real people are more complicated than arguments.
And the Gospel is deeper than slogans.
Consider the Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated “repentance.”
It refers to a change of mind or understanding that, in the biblical call to repentance, involves turning toward God and a transformed life.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It is not performing public humiliation to prove you are sorry.
It is turning away from sin and toward the God who calls you into new life.
Jesus proclaimed:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15, KJV
And the Greek word χάρις (charis) means grace, favor, or gift.
Grace is not God's declaration that sin never mattered.
Grace is God's undeserved favor given to people who cannot save themselves.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of our works.
And Ephesians 2:10 continues by saying believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the order?
We are not transformed so that we can purchase grace.
We receive grace, and God's work in us bears fruit in a transformed life.
This is where the conversation about uncomfortable sexual laws becomes much more personal.
Because the Bible is not merely a collection of rules for people who have never failed.
It is the unfolding story of a holy God dealing with a deeply broken humanity.
A humanity that has exploited.
Betrayed.
Lusted.
Manipulated.
Abused.
Lied.
Hidden.
And sometimes used religion itself to cover the damage.
But Scripture also reveals a God who hears the cries of the oppressed, judges wickedness, calls sinners to repentance, and makes redemption possible through Jesus Christ.
The Bible does not conceal the sexual failures of its own prominent characters.
David's actions involving Bathsheba in 2 Samuel 11 are not presented as a beautiful romance.
David was king.
He possessed extraordinary power.
He sent for Bathsheba, who was married to Uriah.
The narrative does not give us grounds to assume that her participation was freely chosen under those circumstances.
And David subsequently arranged Uriah's death.
The prophet Nathan confronted David.
Second Samuel 12:9 asks why David despised the word of the Lord by doing evil.
David's royal status did not make his conduct righteous.
His place in the biblical story did not excuse him.
And when he confessed his sin, the consequences did not simply disappear.
That matters.
Because a person can receive forgiveness and still be accountable for the harm they have caused.
A ministry leader can preach truth and still commit evil.
A respected Christian can quote Scripture and still be guilty of abuse.
And a church can speak loudly about sexual morality while failing terribly at protecting those who have been harmed.
When that happens, the answer is not to abandon truth.
It is to stop selectively applying it.
Judgment must not be reserved for the powerless while the influential receive protection.
And repentance must never become a public relations strategy.
Now think about the woman at the well in John 4.
Jesus meets a Samaritan woman and speaks to her about living water.
He knows the history of her relationships.
He tells her she has had five husbands and that the man she now has is not her husband.
The passage does not explain why those marriages ended.
It does not tell us whether she had been widowed, divorced, abandoned, or mistreated.
So we should not invent a scandalous sexual biography for her simply because her marital history was complicated.
That is one of the very mistakes careful Bible reading should correct.
Jesus knows the truth about her life.
Yet He still speaks with her.
He still offers living water.
He still reveals His identity as Messiah.
And the woman goes to her community and invites others to meet Him.
“Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?” — John 4:29, KJV
What a moment.
A woman whose life Jesus knew became a witness who brought others to hear Him.
Not because her past was irrelevant.
But because her encounter with Christ became more important than the assumptions people might make about her.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to hear.
You are not beyond the reach of Jesus because your story is complicated.
You are not disqualified from seeking Him because your marriage failed.
You are not worthless because someone violated your trust.
You are not permanently defined by a sexual sin you have repented of.
And you are not required to pretend your choices were righteous in order to believe that God can forgive you.
The Gospel does not say that nothing happened.
It says that Jesus Christ entered a world where terrible things happen, bore our sins, died, and rose again so that sinners might be reconciled to God.
First Peter 2:24 says Christ bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sins and live unto righteousness.
That is not cheap grace.
It cost the Son of God His life.
And when He rose from the dead, He did not merely offer a way to feel better about the past.
He opened the way to a new life.
This is why Christians cannot read the Bible's difficult sexual laws as though Jesus never came.
The New Testament teaches that Christians are not under the Mosaic covenant as Israel was.
Hebrews 8:13 speaks of the old covenant becoming obsolete in relation to the new.
Acts 15 records the early church wrestling with which requirements should be placed upon Gentile believers.
Galatians warns against making observance of the Mosaic Law the basis of justification.
Yet the New Testament also calls Christians to sexual holiness, faithfulness, self-control, love, and justice.
First Corinthians 6:18 calls believers to flee sexual immorality.
First Thessalonians 4:3–5 connects sanctification with abstaining from sexual immorality and learning self-control.
These commands are not an invitation to despise the body.
They are part of the Christian understanding that our bodies matter to God.
That sexual behavior has moral significance.
That people are never merely objects for another person's appetite.
And that grace does not leave us unchanged.
The Christian sexual ethic must therefore be studied from the whole witness of Scripture, with attention to covenant, context, language, and the teaching of Christ and His apostles.
Not by selecting one ancient law and announcing that it answers every modern question.
Not by dismissing difficult passages whenever they challenge us.
And not by pretending that every interpretive disagreement is proof of bad faith.
Sometimes faithfulness requires admitting:
“I need to study this more carefully.”
Those words are not a defeat.
They may be the beginning of wisdom.
Perhaps the most uncomfortable truth in this entire discussion is that some Christians have been more afraid of admitting a passage is difficult than of misrepresenting it.
We wanted answers that would fit into a thirty-second video.
We wanted a Hebrew word that would make every controversy disappear.
We wanted to tell the skeptic that there was no problem.
We wanted to tell the wounded believer that every ancient law was obviously protective.
But Scripture deserves better than that.
And people deserve better than that.
The Bible was written across centuries, in different literary genres, languages, cultures, and covenantal settings.
Its meaning cannot always be reduced to a convenient slogan.
Context does not erase moral difficulty.
Sometimes context explains a problem.
Sometimes it limits a misunderstanding.
Sometimes it exposes assumptions we did not realize we were bringing to the text.
And sometimes, even after careful study, serious questions remain.
A mature Christian faith should be capable of acknowledging that.
Because our confidence is not built upon the claim that every passage is immediately simple.
Our confidence is ultimately in Jesus Christ.
The One who called sinners to repentance.
The One who confronted religious hypocrisy.
The One who showed compassion to the vulnerable.
The One who refused to compromise truth for popularity.
The One who gave His life for our salvation.
The One who rose again.
And the One who is worthy of our trust even while we continue learning how to read His Word faithfully.
Maybe you began this article hoping for ammunition against critics.
Maybe you came because you are the critic.
Maybe someone used these passages to wound you.
Maybe you have been avoiding them for years.
Or maybe you simply want to love God with your heart, soul, strength, and mind, and you are tired of shallow answers.
Wherever you began, I hope you leave with something deeper than an argument.
I hope you leave with a renewed commitment to truth.
A truth that does not need to hide difficult verses.
A truth that does not sacrifice compassion.
A truth that refuses to excuse abuse.
A truth that calls sin by its name.
A truth that understands ancient laws in their ancient setting.
And a truth that finds its fulfillment not in our ability to win debates, but in the person and work of Jesus Christ.
If this article exposed an assumption you have held about Scripture, be honest about it.
If it reminded you of someone who was wounded by careless religious teaching, remember them with compassion.
If it convicted you about the way you have treated others, do not bury that conviction.
Bring it before God.
And if you are still struggling with the difficult passages, you do not have to pretend your questions have vanished.
You can keep studying.
You can seek wise teachers.
You can read serious biblical scholarship.
You can pray.
And you can refuse to let fear dictate your interpretation.
And if you have a thoughtful question about one of these passages, bring it into the conversation.
Not to attack someone.
Not to score points.
But because careful questions can help an entire community grow.
You may have a friend who is quietly losing confidence in Scripture because no one has taken their questions seriously.
You may know a believer who has confused defending God with defending abusive behavior.
You may know someone who thinks following Jesus requires switching off their mind.
Let them encounter a different kind of conversation.
Not because every post will answer every question.
But because we want to keep opening Scripture, pointing people to Jesus Christ, and encouraging genuine discipleship.
Those resources are intended to help people go beyond a passing emotional reaction and develop a lasting habit of studying God's Word.
And if this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, return to prayer, confront sin, or draw closer to Christ, I want to invite you to consider something.
But I want to make something clear.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That means your giving should come from conviction, freedom, and generosity—not guilt.
Your responsibilities to your family, your local church, and those in genuine need matter.
Those items are simply an expression of appreciation.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
More biblical nourishment.
More thoughtful engagement with Scripture.
More encouragement for people who are struggling.
More opportunities to proclaim the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Your prayers matter.
Your willingness to study matters.
Your commitment to truth matters.
Your compassion toward wounded people matters.
And your desire to glorify Christ matters far more than any financial contribution.
Because the mission was never supposed to be about building an audience that merely applauds religious content.
It is about helping people encounter the truth of God's Word and the grace of Jesus Christ.
A skeptic may begin reading because of an uncomfortable law.
A wounded believer may keep reading because someone finally acknowledged the pain.
A struggling Christian may discover that repentance is still possible.
And someone who has been hiding in shame may remember that the risen Savior still calls sinners to Himself.
That is the Gospel we must never lose.
Not a Gospel that excuses sin.
Not a Gospel that ignores suffering.
Not a Gospel that demands unquestioning loyalty to human institutions.
But the Gospel of the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
The One who does not need our dishonest defenses.
The One who calls us to walk in truth.
The One whose grace is powerful enough to forgive sinners and transform lives.
And the One who will never require us to call darkness light in order to honor His name.

Because the deepest scandal is not that the Bible records humanity's brokenness—it is that the sinless Savior entered our broken world and gave His life to redeem people who could never rescue themselves.
